01

Gear shaft for an 80 HP gearbox

Sized, toleranced and drew a shaft carrying two spur gears at 600 rpm, then checked the design against a finite element model.

Course
MECH 325, Colorado State University
Team
Lucas Barnes, Gabe Klarenbach, Jonathan Bannerot
Material
AISI 1020 hot-rolled steel
Loads
80 HP at 600 rpm, 8,403 lbf-in torque, 4,902 lbf-in peak bending moment
Tools
SolidWorks, MATLAB, FEBio
2.5minimum fatigue and yield safety factor required
2.6lowest fatigue safety factor across the six checked locations
51,500 hrcalculated bearing life, against a 10,000 to 25,000 hr target
Read the full write-up

The problem

An 80 HP drive delivers power to gear D from shaft AB. Shaft CD runs at 600 rpm and carries a 20 in gear (D) and an 8 in gear (C), both 20 degree spur gears. The shaft is meant for a consumer vehicle gearbox, so it needed a 10,000 to 25,000 hour life, and every critical section needed a safety factor of at least 2.5 for both fatigue and yield.

What we did

  1. Loads. Found the tangential and radial gear forces (840 and 306 lbf at gear D, 2,101 and 765 lbf at gear C), the bearing reactions, and shear and moment diagrams in two planes. The combined bending moment peaks at 4,902 lbf-in at gear C.
  2. Material. Chose 1020 hot-rolled steel for cost, availability and machinability.
  3. Diameters. Estimated the diameter at the limiting shoulder, then checked every shoulder, retaining ring groove and keyway with stress concentration factors, including Neuber's constant, and Goodman fatigue and yield safety factors. Locations f, g and h share geometry with c, d and e but see lower moment, so they were not repeated.
  4. Keys and rings. Sized a 5/8 by 7/16 in square key, 1.85 in long, from shear and bearing stress, and picked retaining rings with grooves cut to the manufacturer's dimensions.
  5. Bearings. Selected an SKF C 2206 TN9 cylindrical roller bearing because the loads are radial, checked its L10 life, and specified a locational interference fit (H7/p6) on the 30 mm bearing seats.
  6. Documents. Produced the dimensioned drawing and the assembly drawing in SolidWorks.

Safety factors by location

LocationFeatureDiameterFatigueYield
aShoulder at bearing1.18 in2.65.2
bShoulder2.00 in3.67.8
cRetaining ring groove2.75 in5.312.0
dKeyway, gear C2.75 in2.73.2
eShoulder at gear C2.75 in3.13.9
iShoulder at bearing1.18 in4.28.7

Where the FEA disagreed

At point i, the finite element model predicted a von Mises stress of about 46,000 psi (yield safety factor 0.87), while the hand calculation gave 4,850 psi (safety factor 8.7). We put the gap down to how we set up the model: the loads were applied as pressure and traction patches on geometry built from a MATLAB script, without modeling the gear and bearing contact, and the mesh convergence study didn't settle cleanly. The model did put the peak stress at the shoulder and keyway where the hand analysis expects stress concentrations, but I would not use its magnitudes. Next time I would model the contact properly and compare against the hand calculations before trusting the FEA.

What I would change

Our own reflection was that the retaining rings are the weak point. They can slip when tolerances stack up, and every groove weakens the shaft. The keyway also stops short of the shaft end, so a gear has to be forced over the shaft surface before it reaches the keyway, which can damage both parts. Shaft collars would simplify manufacturing and remove the grooves, with the keyways adjusted to suit.

02

Timed pill dispenser

A portable dispenser that attaches to a water bottle, holds four medications, and releases them at up to 16 programmable times a day.

Course
MECH 307, final report May 2026
Team
James Tharp, Lucas Barnes, Jonathan Bannerot
Controller
Arduino Nano ESP32, DS3231 real-time clock
Hardware
OLED display, 2 MG90S servos, 4 IR break-beam sensor pairs, buzzer, 3 buttons, potentiometer
Made with
SolidWorks, 3D printing, C++ on Arduino
16programmable dispense times: four pills, four times each
6 of 6functional subsystems met their requirements
2servos drive all four pill slots
Read the full write-up

How it works

The user sets dispense times for each of the four pill slots with two buttons and a menu on the OLED. When a scheduled time arrives, a buzzer chimes and the screen alerts the user. Pressing the dispense button runs one or both servos, which turn a gear that drives a plunger to push a pill out of its vertical slot into a pull-out tray on the left or right side. An LED shows which tray received the pills.

Four IR break-beam sensor pairs watch the fill level of each slot. When a slot drops to roughly three pills, the beam is no longer blocked and the screen shows a refill message for that slot. Each slot has a sliding door for reloading and a spring stopper at the top to keep the sensor readings consistent. A potentiometer sets how often the chime beeps and can turn it off.

The software

The main loop reads the clock, polls the sensors and compares the time with every saved schedule. A flag stops the same schedule from firing twice in one minute. Because several functions want the screen at once, the code uses a priority order: dispensing first, then menus, then refill warnings, then the clock. That kept messages from overwriting one another.

Results

The finished device met the requirements for all six subsystems. The dispensing mechanism worked consistently, with very few jams, and those cleared with a slight shake of the device.

What was hard

Sliding parts were the hardest to tolerance. Getting the pill doors to move freely without letting a pill slip out took many print iterations, each costing hours, and it depended on print orientation and supports as much as on clearances. Parts designed by different teammates also collided in the assembly until we started meeting regularly and sharing models. On the electronics side, the OLED and clock both use I2C, which we hadn't covered in class, so we had to learn the wiring, libraries and setup on our own.

03

Beverage lift: from four-bar linkage to cylindrical cam

A one-motor device that raises a 12 oz can 29 inches to desk height for people who can't easily bend down, redesigned from a six-foot linkage into a 34-inch cam.

Course
MECH 324, three-part project
Team
Lucas Barnes, Brenden Engbers, Jonathan Bannerot
Motion
29 in rise, 30 s per cycle, pausing at the bottom and the top
Drive
One motor, 24 V brushed DC gear motor (7.2 W)
Tools
SolidWorks, MATLAB
6 ft to 34 inoverall height, first linkage design against the final cam
29 inrise, with a pause at each end to load and unload the can
4.4 Wpeak power at a 30 s cycle, against 39.6 W if sped up to 10 s
Read the full write-up

The need

Someone with a back injury or limited mobility shouldn't have to bend down to a mini fridge. The device takes a can from the floor to the height of a desk with the push of a button. The requirements were to fit in a 6.5 by 3 by 1 ft space against a wall, lift 30 inches, and use a single motor.

Part 1: a linkage that grew too tall

We started with a crank-slider, using two-position synthesis: a 15 in crank, half of the 30 in stroke, and a 50 in coupler. Because a crank-slider doesn't fit the usual Grashof test directly, we classified it at the fully retracted and fully extended positions. The first version could only move straight up. The second tilted the slider to add horizontal travel and used a spring-and-pin cap that clips onto a can to pick it up and release it.

Sizing the links was the hard part. To reach both corners of the slot path and still turn a full revolution without hitting a toggle position, we had to adjust link lengths in very small steps over many attempts.

Part 2: why a cam

The can needs to pause at the bottom to be placed and at the top to be taken. A cam gives you those dwells directly, and a cylindrical cam has the smallest footprint of the options. We analyzed position, velocity, acceleration and jerk in MATLAB and tested two variables: the cycle period and the rise height.

Period (29 in rise)Peak velocityPeak accelerationPeak jerk
15 s11.6 in/s5.67 in/s²14.3 in/s³
30 s5.8 in/s1.42 in/s²1.78 in/s³
45 s3.87 in/s0.63 in/s²0.53 in/s³
Rise (30 s period)Peak velocityPeak accelerationPeak jerk
14 in2.8 in/s0.68 in/s²0.86 in/s³
29 in5.8 in/s1.42 in/s²1.78 in/s³
44 in8.8 in/s2.15 in/s²2.70 in/s³

We kept the 29 in rise because it meets the requirement and a taller rise raises acceleration and jerk. A slower cycle lowers all three, so we settled on 30 seconds, since nobody needs a fresh can every 10 seconds. The new design has four parts (the cam, a roller, a support pole and a slotted platform) and stands 34 inches tall instead of nearly six feet.

Part 3: forces and the motor

We treated the roller as a ball rolling up an incline: the pressure angle comes from the slope of the displacement curve, and the can and coupler weight gives the vertical and horizontal forces on the cam, then torque and power. To keep the analysis tractable we assumed no friction between the coupler and the pole, and we applied the can's weight on the way down too, which adds margin.

  • Baseline, steel coupler, 30 s: peak horizontal force about 53 lbf, vertical about 2.7 lbf, peak power 4.4 W.
  • Faster, 10 s: peak horizontal force about 160 lbf and 39.6 W. Rejected, because forces and motor size jumped for no real benefit.
  • Acrylic coupler, 30 s: about 23 lbf and 1.9 W. Rejected, because we worried it could fail under a full can.
  • Motor: a 24 V brushed DC gear motor rated 7.2 W covers the 4.4 W peak and costs less than a brushless option.

Trade-offs and what's missing

Switching from a linkage to a cam shrank the machine and simplified the motion, but it gave up the pick-and-place function of the first design. The can now has to be put on the platform by another mechanism, such as a spring-loaded dispenser fed from a mini fridge. The physical prototype was specified as a 5:1 scale print that raises a can 6 inches. If I did the linkage again, I would choose a mechanism where link lengths are less critical, since that precision leads to tolerance problems when you actually build it.

04

How long should a drink sit in the freezer?

A heat transfer model, solved in MATLAB, that predicts how long a 12 oz can needs to reach 4 °C in a household freezer, tested against a real can.

Course
MECH 344, Heat and Mass Transfer
Project
Individual final project
Question
Time for a 12 oz can to cool from 25 °C to 4 °C in a −18 °C freezer
Model
Lumped capacitance with convection, radiation and shelf conduction
Tools
MATLAB, ode45
40.5 minpredicted time to reach 4 °C
9.9 °Cmeasured at that time, against 4.0 °C predicted
19.6 Winitial heat removal: 40% convection, 36% shelf, 24% radiation
Read the full write-up

Setting up the problem

I measured the can with calipers (65 mm diameter, 123 mm tall), treated the drink as water, and modeled the freezer as a well-mixed space at −18 °C. The inputs I could not measure were the fan airflow (estimated at 0.3 m/s), the fraction of time the fan runs (assumed 65%), the shelf conductivity (0.20 W/m·K) and the can's emissivity (0.8).

The model

  1. Convection. Forced convection with the fan on came from the Churchill-Bernstein cross-flow correlation (Re about 1,430, h = 7.28 W/m²·K). Natural convection with the fan off came from a Rayleigh number correlation (h = 4.66 W/m²·K). I weighted them by the duty cycle to get an effective h of 6.36 W/m²·K.
  2. Radiation. The can is a small body in a large enclosure, so the exchange reduces to the one-body formula with the can's emissivity.
  3. Shelf conduction. The can's bottom sits on a 4 mm plastic shelf, so it is left out of the convection and radiation areas and exchanges heat only through the shelf (0.166 W/K).
  4. Aluminum wall. Its thermal resistance was a few millionths of the convective resistance, so I dropped it.
  5. Lumped capacitance. The Biot number came out at 0.14, slightly above the usual 0.1 limit. I accepted the approximation because natural convection inside the liquid keeps it fairly well mixed, and I said so in the report.
  6. Solving it. Because radiation depends on T⁴, the energy balance has no closed-form solution, so I integrated it with ode45 and ran a sweep of fan duty cycles from 10% to 100%.

The model missed by about 6 °C

I pulled the can out at the predicted 40.5 minutes and measured 9.9 °C, not 4.0 °C, so the real can cooled more slowly than the model said. The largest uncertainties were my own estimates of fan speed and duty cycle, then the emissivity and shelf conductivity. With only one trial, I can't separate model error from measurement error. The next steps I would take are measuring the fan airflow directly, modeling the fan as an explicit on-off cycle instead of a time average, and measuring the shelf's actual conductivity.

What the model says about real freezers

Convection is the largest single term, but shelf conduction takes about 36% of the initial heat load. Setting the can on a wire rack instead of a plastic shelf would therefore slow cooling noticeably, while setting it on a metal shelf would speed it up a lot.

05

Crane structure sized by hand, MATLAB and FEA

Chose steel sections for a four-member crane so every member clears a 2.5 safety factor using as little material as possible.

Course
MECH 325, Project 1
Team
Lucas Barnes, Gabe Klarenbach, Jonathan Bannerot
Material
AISI 1018 hot-rolled steel
Load
10 kN at the boom tip
Tools
MATLAB, SolidWorks, FEBio
10candidate sections screened: five W-beams, five square HSS
2.63lowest hand-calculated safety factor in the final design
6meshes in the convergence study
Read the full write-up

Approach

  1. Statics. Solved the reaction forces in all six members, drew shear and moment diagrams for the boom and mast, and used Mohr's circle at each critical point to get principal and maximum shear stresses.
  2. Section selection in MATLAB. Screened five W-beams and five square HSS sections, converting everything to mm, mm² and mm⁴ and computing bending, axial and total stress and the factor of safety for each. We picked the section with the lowest safety factor still above 2.5 for each member, which keeps material and cost down.
  3. Result. A W-beam with a 333 mm depth and 313 mm flange width for the mast and boom, and an HSS square section for the two brace members. The governing safety factors were 2.63 (member AC) and 2.94 (the mast).
  4. FEA. Built a single continuous model in FEBio with the material at 205 GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.29, fixed the base, applied the 10 kN load as a surface traction at the boom tip, and ran a six-mesh convergence study. Across the five finest meshes, strain energy changed by less than about 1.3% from one mesh to the next.

Hand calculations against FEA

MemberHand FOSFEA FOS
AC (brace)2.6316.4
BE (mast)2.9427.0
DF (brace)4.075.98
EG (boom)13.954.1

Reading the difference

The FEA safety factors came out well above the hand values, so the hand calculation is the conservative one. One likely reason is that the FEA treated the crane as a single continuous body, while the hand calculation assumed pin-jointed members and looked only at the worst point of each. I would run a model with pinned joints to confirm that before leaning on either number.

Why W-beams

For a steel with moderate yield strength, the sections have to be large to hold the stresses down. W-beams put their material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, so they resist bending well for their weight, and they are cheap, standardized and easy to order. The trade-offs are lower torsional stiffness than HSS and a tendency to buckle locally under compression.

Why it matters

The sheets build in the checks a machinist would otherwise learn the hard way: take the chuck key out, measure with calipers because the DRO isn't always accurate, and verify indexing with a trial notch before committing to full depth. It's the same documentation habit I want to bring to production work.

More work

Smaller projects, course work and writing where I learned a process or practiced a design method.

Bat Bot: StrongRAM 2025 competition robot

MECH 202 · Team of four: Gavin Horvath, Lucas Barnes, Brenden Engbers, Zachary Hollema

A Batman Tumbler-styled robot built to push a truck, lift a lacrosse ball onto a pedestal, flip flagpoles and hang from a chin-up bar. It has two driven wheels and two casters, a 3D-printed chassis redesigned three times, a chain-and-scoop lift that handles both the ball and the flagpoles, and a two-servo arm for the chin-up. We started with a belt-driven lift, found the belts either too stiff or too stretchy, and switched to bike chain. We stayed under both our electronics and non-electronics budgets.

The chin-up arm never held the robot fully off the ground before the deadline. We ran out of time and budget to fix it, and the report says so.

When should an R&D team 3D print, and when should it machine?

JTC 300, Strategic Writing and Communication · 20-page position and recommendation report · May 2026

I reviewed peer-reviewed and government research on additive manufacturing (AM) in R&D and argued for a middle path: use AM as the main tool for early prototyping, where speed, design freedom and low tooling cost win, and plan the handoff to traditional methods for validation, load-bearing and fatigue-critical parts, and higher quantities. Rather than picking a side, the report recommends a criteria-based decision framework and a repeatable workflow.

  • Where AM wins: no fixtures or toolpaths, so a design can change in the morning and be tested the next day, and the cost per part stays nearly flat at small quantities.
  • Where it loses: cost per part overtakes machining as quantities grow, printed metal can behave differently along and across the build direction and often needs post-processing, and machining still holds tighter tolerances and finishes.
  • Stated limits: the report uses secondary sources only and no cost data from a real organization, so the crossover points will differ from case to case.
CriterionFavors 3D printingFavors traditional methods
Geometric complexityInternal channels, lattices, organic shapesSimple prismatic or rotational parts
Expected quantity1 to 10 unitsAbove the cost crossover point
Design stabilityFrequent iteration expectedDesign locked, repeat production planned
Lead timeHours to a few daysWeeks available for tooling and setup
Mechanical criticalityForm, fit and function checksCertified load-bearing or fatigue-critical parts
Dimensional tolerance±0.1 mm acceptable with post-processingTight as-built tolerance, below ±0.05 mm
The six-phase workflow
  1. Scope. Classify the prototype as a concept model, form-and-fit check, functional prototype or pre-production article, and state the mechanical, thermal and dimensional requirements up front.
  2. Screen. Score the prototype against the criteria above and route it to printing or to machining or an outside vendor.
  3. Pilot. Run the first build conservatively and record orientation, scan strategy and any heat treatment so the result can be reproduced.
  4. Validate. Inspect dimensions and, where structure matters, test witness coupons printed alongside the part.
  5. Decide. Document whether the printed part works as is, needs post-processing, or should be re-sourced for the next iteration.
  6. Review. Revisit the decision each quarter as materials, printers and qualification data change.

The recommendation also covers training engineers on both processes and keeping a machine shop next to any industrial printer, since one complements the other.

Outlet timer teardown

MECH 202 · Zachary Hollema and Lucas Barnes

Took apart a BN-LINK mechanical outlet timer and documented it: a 21-part bill of materials with materials and likely manufacturing processes, disassembly steps, interfaces, a design structure matrix and customer requirements drawn from product reviews. Then scored three upgrades against the original with a weighted Pugh matrix: a glow-in-the-dark dial (3.05 against a 3.00 baseline), multiple outlets (2.95) and Bluetooth (2.75).

Screwdrivers: forged versus molded

Introduction to manufacturing

Made one screwdriver by drop forging, heat treating and machining a tool steel blade with a knurled handle, and one with an injection-molded handle. Costing both showed the point of process choice: about $231 and 11 hours of labor for the forged one, against about $7 and 15 minutes for the molded one. My proposal for the forged version was to fold the knurling into the CNC lathe and automate the forging.

Clock: manual mill and lathe

Introduction to manufacturing

A desk clock with pen and pencil holders, machined from brass, steel and aluminum on manual machines. It took about 30 hours and cost roughly $646 in materials and labor. Reworking the plan around a CNC lathe and mill and a laser-cut face brought my estimate down to about 3 hours and $106 per clock, around six times cheaper. The lesson I kept: rushing a manual operation always cost me more time than slowing down.
